## The questions of the five analysts {#five-analysts-five-questions .smaller}

::: {.fs-70}
| Analyst | Level of analysis in Task 2 | Estimator in Task 2 | Question of the free phase |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| 018OL | 420 cells of country, year and wave | random intercepts for country, year and wave | GDP per capita on the mean of the seven positive items |
| KEVF1 | 209,826 respondents | random intercepts for countries and years within countries | GDP growth on the sum of the seven positive items |
| PRL47 | 394,575 respondents | three levels, random slopes, individual and national controls | GDP per capita, growth and a crisis dummy on three positive shares |
| KQXUE | 270 country-years | a fixed effect for each country | GDP growth and unemployment on the cosmopolitan and utilitarian shares |
| **C6HJR** | 270 country-years | fixed effects for country and year | GDP growth and unemployment on the share of the seven positive items |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
- Five free analyses, five different questions, and **one shared verdict**, 'evidence for the claim'; three of the five never used the unemployment rate
- Analysts who look as though they disagree are often answering different questions, which is why Lundberg and colleagues ask every study "What is your estimand?" [@LundbergEtAl2021WhatYourEstimand]
:::

::: {.src}
The Multi100 record (osf.io/q5h2c) and the public code of the analysts, read on the [case page]({{< var site-url >}}cases/eu-frames/index.html#sec-reanalysts); @AuspurgBruderl2021HasCredibilitySocial on the red-card study.
:::

::: notes
Before you write your own, look at what the five of us did in the free first task. GDP per capita for one, GDP growth for another, GDP measures with a crisis dummy for a third, and three of the five never touched the unemployment rate. The outcomes differ too, a mean, a sum, a share, three separate shares, and so do the units: two of us on respondents, one on cells of a country in one wave, two on country-years. Those are five different questions, and every one of us recorded the same verdict, evidence for the claim. [advance] Auspurg and Brüderl found the same thing in the twenty-nine teams of the red-card study: much of what looks like analytical disagreement is unstated disagreement about what is being estimated. Lundberg and colleagues put the remedy in the title of their paper, what is your estimand, and that is what you write now.
:::

## The estimand statement {#the-estimand-statement}

::: {.claimcard}
"The expected change in [unit quantity] among [target population] for a 1-percentage-point difference in unemployment, holding [assumptions] fixed."
:::

::: {.small}
- Unit quantity – a *person's* cosmopolitan framing, or a *country-year* mean?
- Target population – which countries, which years?
- Held fixed – the stable traits of a country, the shocks of a year, the other measure of the economy?
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Now:** your one-sentence estimand for the claim. Write it, hold it, and send it when I say go.
:::

::: {.src}
The template follows @LundbergEtAl2021WhatYourEstimand.
:::

::: notes
Fill in the brackets of the statement on the slide: your one-sentence estimand for the claim. Is the unit quantity the framing of a person or the mean of a country-year? Which countries and years are the population? What do you hold fixed: the stable traits of a country, whatever every country went through in a year, the other measure of the economy? Write it, hold it, and send it when I say go. [go; read three or four aloud] Look at the spread. Some of you wrote about the framing of a person, some about a country-year average, some named different years or different things held fixed. None of those statements is wrong. They are different questions, and the coefficient means something different in each: the disagreement of the five free analyses in miniature. Keep your statement for the second half.
:::
